extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, patent examiners, legal scholars, and policymakers interested in claim construction and prosecution practice
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria for how claims should be interpreted and prosecuted to promote public notice, including the broadest reasonable construction rule, examiner practices, prior-art search obligations, and incentives for precise drafting. Focuses on prosecution-stage standards and their effects in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the public record to determine claim meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should rely on the public record (claims, specification, prosecution history) to determine what the patent does and does not claim and to resolve vague terms, rather than extrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article explains that testimony (including patentee testimony) is given little weight and that extrinsic evidence is disfavored because it risks changing claim meaning 'in derogation of the indisputable public records consisting of the claims, the specification and the prosecution history.' Example citations: Phillips v. AWH Corp.; courts prefer using the public record to aid public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret claims to incentivize precise initial claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be interpreted in a manner that creates incentives for applicants to draft precise claims in their initial applications to reduce uncertainty in claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretive approach aims to motivate ex ante clarity by imposing costs (e.g., rejections) on vague claims so applicants choose clearer language up front. The Article links this to the idea of a 'penalty default' that increases the cost ex post if clarity is absent, but notes practical limits to the incentive (applicants may lack resources or information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against broad constructions that ensnare unwary infringers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous claims should presumptively not be construed broadly if such a construction would 'ensnare unwary infringers' or improperly expand claim scope leading to invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply a presumption favoring narrower readings of ambiguous claims in litigation to protect potential infringers and avoid granting unjustifiably broad post-issuance scope. The Article cites Athletic Alternatives v. Prince Mfg. and discusses this presumption as one of three claim-interpretation approaches supporting public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Construction (BRC) during prosecution to promote iterative clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: During prosecution, claims should be given the broadest reasonable construction to encourage rejection of imprecise claims, prompting applicants to amend and thereby create a clearer public record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article states the BRC was created to (1) generate clarifying amendments and a developed prosecution record through iterative rejections, (2) induce more precise initial drafting, and (3) fix an outer limit for claims. Example: In re Bigio — BRC led to rejection based on toothbrush prior art and forced Bigio to amend a claim to 'hair brush for a person’s head or scalp.' The Article also notes limits: examiners may still allow broad claims due to inadequate prior art or differing understandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRC as an ex ante 'penalty default' to create drafting incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: The BRC should function like a penalty default: by imposing a costly consequence (broad construction leading to rejection) on vague claims, applicants are incentivized ex ante to draft narrower, clearer claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article explains the theoretical similarity to economic penalty defaults but notes empirical failures: the cost of iterative prosecution does not reliably induce precise initial drafting, applicants may gamble, and the rule’s effect depends on examiner practice and search quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRC to fix outer limits of claim scope (prevent later expansion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the USPTO applies the broadest reasonable construction at prosecution and states its understanding clearly, that construction can serve as a fixed outer boundary so courts will not later construe claims more broadly in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In theory this prevents unwary infringers from being later caught by broader litigation interpretations. In practice, the Article finds this effect limited because courts sometimes construe claims more broadly than the USPTO, and appellate reversal/modification rates for claim constructions are high (cited empirical statistics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative improvements via rejection-and-amendment process
rubrics_metrics.description: A healthy prosecution process should produce iterative improvements: broad constructions cause rejections, applicants amend to clarify, and the resulting prosecution history clarifies claim scope for the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article describes how iterative rejection/amendment builds a written record showing what the applicant/examiner believe the claims mean (and do not mean). However, it notes practical barriers: examiners often exercise broad discretion, may not suggest corrective language, and applicants alone determine amendments—so iterative improvements can be incomplete or produce new ambiguities (Bigio example where some claims were clarified while others issued broadly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must conduct adequate prior art searches (limitations noted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective application of BRC presumes examiners perform adequate prior-art searches so that broad constructions will surface relevant art to prompt rejections of overbroad claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article documents limits on examiners' searches: resource/time constraints; statutory/search-method mismatch (statute covers prior use but examiners focus on printed publications); prohibition on using 'common knowledge and common sense'; limits on Internet searches pre-publication. Inadequate searches can allow vague, broad claims to issue as 'valid' and undermine public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete review of specification, dependent claims, and prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should thoroughly review the specification, dependent claims, and prosecution history because these materials bear on claim scope and can disclose disclaimers limiting claim meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under BRC, examiners often fail to identify disclaimers or nuances in dependent claims; dependent claims receive less scrutiny because they are assumed narrower than independent claims. The Article gives Inpro II as an example where failure to address ambiguity (parallel vs. serial interface) at prosecution led to expensive litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize dependent claims and new claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not assume dependent claims are automatically acceptable whenever the independent claim is allowable; new language in dependent claims may affect search scope and requires independent scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that the presumption that dependent claims are patentable if the parent is patentable can leave ambiguities untested until litigation, because added dependent limitations could change the relevant prior-art search or claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize BRC functions more like a standard than a bright-line rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The BRC often functions as a standard that leaves substantial discretion to examiners, rather than a precise rule that yields consistent, predictable constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article argues examiners must use judgment to determine what words mean, producing variability. It cites the rule-vs-standard literature and notes the resulting uncertainty undermines ex ante influence on applicants and contributes to inconsistent prosecution outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for applicant-side limits on producing clarity (incentives and abilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether applicants have incentives, drafting skill, and resources to produce clear claims—lack of these can prevent the BRC from causing ex ante clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article notes patentees may not write well, may lack funds, or may not think the patent justifies investment in specificity. Applicants are not required to search for prior art before filing; the initial claim language reflects their beliefs, and they often await examiner search results before amending. Duty of candor (37 C.F.R. §1.56) exists, but applicants control amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts in litigation will often construe claims more narrowly to preserve validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because courts cannot amend claims post-issuance, in litigation they may construe claims narrowly (to save validity), and thus cannot rely on the prosecution-stage iterative or penalty-default mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article explains courts' limited ability to clarify claims after issuance justifies using different interpretive rules in litigation than during prosecution; cites cases (In re Etter, Athletic Alternatives, Phillips) and explains that reliance on post-issuance narrowing can protect alleged infringers but reduces the BRC's effectiveness in fixing outer claim limits.
